title: Black Light Attack!

jokes.text: hey, kenneth, why aren't your teeth glowing in the black light? / you'll have to ask the fella who whittled 'em for me.
jokes.setup: At an afterparty under black lights, Tracy notices Kenneth's teeth aren't glowing like normal teeth would.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth casually reveals his teeth were hand-carved by someone — implying they're wooden or artificial, delivered with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: A cold open gem. The setup is visually sharp (black light party) and the punchline reveals something deeply wrong with Kenneth's rural background through the most specific possible detail — 'whittled.' The word choice is perfect. Only Kenneth could deliver this with absolute sincerity. High craft: maximum funny per word, completely character-specific, and the image of whittled teeth is original and surreal.

jokes.text: i want to be tgs' steve nash. come down from canada, work hard, make the black guy look good.
jokes.setup: Jack compliments Danny on being a gentleman and says it's good to have 'another one of us around.' Danny responds with his personal career aspiration.
jokes.punchline: Danny explicitly frames his role as supporting Tracy (the Black star) by referencing Steve Nash, the white Canadian NBA player known for facilitating Black teammates' success — with complete self-aware honesty.
jokes.explanation: A very sharp racial self-awareness joke that works on multiple levels: Danny's Canadian background, the basketball analogy, the frank acknowledgment of racial show business dynamics. The Steve Nash comparison is specific and earned. It's quotable, character-specific, and shows the writers' willingness to go to uncomfortable but smart places. Justifies the 8+ because it's comparable in quality to the 'never go with a hippie' anchor — punchy, specific, quotable.

jokes.text: Good job tonight, danny. Robot lorenzo lamas was funny. as was robot ryan seacrest and david hasselbot.
jokes.setup: Characters congratulate Danny on the show. The 'robot' sketches are listed.
jokes.punchline: 'David Hasselbot' — a portmanteau of David Hasselhoff and 'robot' that perfectly captures the dumb-but-funny sketch comedy energy.
jokes.explanation: 'Hasselbot' is a clean wordplay gag that's brief and funny. The escalating list (Lamas, Seacrest, Hasselhoff) builds with the best pun saved for last. Competent joke construction with a satisfying payoff word.

jokes.text: it's not what you think! it's something i need to wear to support my breasts!
jokes.setup: A character is caught in a compromising position ('oh, boy') apparently wearing something unusual — context suggests he's wearing a bra or similar garment.
jokes.punchline: The explanation 'to support my breasts' is more alarming than whatever was imagined, delivered desperately.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual gag with a misdirection punchline — the explanation makes things worse, not better. Standard sitcom fare executed competently. The 'support my breasts' line is funny in isolation but doesn't have strong character integration.

jokes.text: lemon, i have season tickets to every sports team in new york. so close to the action, you'll feel like you're sitting in front of an hd television. And they're wasted on you and your coworkers.
jokes.setup: Jack is complaining to Liz that he has incredible sports tickets.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is the comparison to sitting in front of an HD television — implying live sports are only as good as TV — and then the contempt of 'wasted on you.'
jokes.explanation: Jack's elitist character shines through. The 'HD television' comparison inverts the luxury (admitting it's as good as TV) while still being condescending. Good character integration — this is very Jack.

jokes.text: why won't they put me on the jumbotron? i've been doing cool stuff all game.
jokes.setup: Liz is at a sports game with elite seats, supposedly appreciating the experience.
jokes.punchline: Her primary concern is jumbotron attention — a deeply uncool, self-conscious thing to care about — delivered as a legitimate grievance.
jokes.explanation: This is a tight character joke — Liz at a fancy game is preoccupied with the most dorky possible concern. 'I've been doing cool stuff all game' is the key line, implying she's been performing for the jumbotron camera rather than watching. Very Liz Lemon. Clean economy.

jokes.text: but my biggest problem with quiddich is, if the snitch is 150 points, why does anyone bother with the quaffle?
jokes.setup: Jack has courtside NBA tickets. Liz is at the game.
jokes.punchline: Liz is complaining about the game mechanics of Quidditch (from Harry Potter) instead of paying attention to the actual basketball game — the sports nerd's wrong-sport tangent.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character joke — Liz uses elite NBA courtside seats to expound on Quidditch game theory, demonstrating her total disinterest in real sports while being passionately interested in fictional ones. The specific detail (150 points for the snitch vs. the quaffle) shows the writers actually thought about the logic. Only Liz would do this. High character integration, good originality for a character bit.

jokes.text: hey, jeter! Are you jealous? i'm with my new boyfriend!
jokes.setup: Liz is at a sports game; Derek Jeter is presumably nearby or visible.
jokes.punchline: Liz tries to make Derek Jeter jealous by announcing she has a boyfriend — implying she has some delusion about a relationship with Jeter, and that Danny's presence constitutes a romantic comeback.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist visual gag — Liz shouting at Jeter to make him jealous fits her delusional self-image comedy perfectly. Broad but character-specific and landing in a funny moment of rapid-fire sports scene beats.

jokes.text: Maybe it's that russian dancer with the tattoos, which is the crazy sex trifecta.
jokes.setup: Jack speculates about which woman Danny is secretly seeing.
jokes.punchline: Jack defines 'the crazy sex trifecta' as Russian + dancer + tattoos — delivered as established sexual taxonomy.
jokes.explanation: Jack's worldly confidence in categorizing women as sexual archetypes is a reliable character note. 'Crazy sex trifecta' is a good coinage. The specificity (Russian, dancer, tattoos) elevates it above generic innuendo.

jokes.text: that girl has a name, jack. we call her 'skankovitch.'
jokes.setup: Liz defends the dancer by saying she has a name.
jokes.punchline: The name they've given her is 'Skankovitch' — a fake Russian-sounding surname that is also a slur — delivered as if it's a respectful correction.
jokes.explanation: The perfect subversion — Liz performs feminist allyship ('that girl has a name') and the punchline exposes her own complicity in the nickname culture. 'Skankovitch' is a great coinage: sounds authentically Russian while being obviously derogatory. The structure is nearly flawless: setup creates moral expectation, punchline destroys it instantly. Quotable and memorable.

jokes.text: and you take your reward. [pause] you take your reward.
jokes.setup: Jack is narrating his seduction fantasy scenario to Liz, escalating toward the 'payoff.'
jokes.punchline: He says 'you take your reward' twice, with apparent relish — a deeply uncomfortable euphemism delivered to his female colleague. The repetition and pause make it worse.
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'you take your reward' with the implied dreamy pause is gloriously uncomfortable. Jack has completely forgotten Liz is in the room. The economy of the euphemism and the double-delivery make it land well. Good cringe comedy.

jokes.text: how drunk are you? / a lot to very.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Danny how drunk he is.
jokes.punchline: 'A lot to very' — a non-grammatical but perfectly expressive answer that captures the feeling of being very drunk.
jokes.explanation: 'A lot to very' is a beautiful piece of drunk-speak — it sounds grammatically wrong but is semantically exactly right. It's highly quotable and perfectly captures drunken non-linear communication. Economy score is near-perfect: three words deliver maximum information and comedy. A mini-classic line.

jokes.text: boy, that robot body paint does not wash off. is it the body paint or is danny just glowing like a beacon of manly camaraderie?
jokes.setup: Liz sees Danny still covered in body paint from the show.
jokes.punchline: She immediately pivots to a romantic/admiring description ('beacon of manly camaraderie') — starting to reveal her attraction to Danny through comedy.
jokes.explanation: The joke plants the seed of Liz's attraction while being funny in its overblown language ('beacon of manly camaraderie'). It's a transitional joke that does narrative and comedic work simultaneously. Decent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: i play tartine gramercy, an heiress to a vermouth fortune and a freshman at nyu.
jokes.setup: Jenna announces she has an audition for Gossip Girl.
jokes.punchline: The character name ('Tartine Gramercy') is absurdly patrician; being an 'heiress to a vermouth fortune' is specific and silly; and being a college freshman at Jenna's age is the slow-burn reveal.
jokes.explanation: 'Tartine Gramercy' and 'vermouth fortune' are great 30 Rock-style name/detail comedy. The freshman college student detail is a plant for the mother-age-denial joke coming later. Good character work for Jenna's vanity and age-delusion theme.

jokes.text: from my treatment of the dancers here to my remarks about madeleine albright at the 1996 white house correspondents' dinner.
jokes.setup: Tracy explains he's had a complicated relationship with women and needs to learn to respect them.
jokes.punchline: He lists two examples of his bad behavior — 'treatment of dancers' (vague but ominous) and a specific insult to Madeleine Albright at the 1996 correspondents' dinner (absurdly specific and historically grounded).
jokes.explanation: The Madeleine Albright reference is beautifully specific — it grounds Tracy's absurdity in a real historical moment. The year (1996) and venue (correspondents' dinner) make it feel like something that actually happened, which is the best kind of Tracy absurdism.

jokes.text: '10:00 a.m. dotcom shows up pictures from his trip to greece.' i think i'm gonna go ahead and cancel that. / okay, i'll reschedule... Again.
jokes.setup: Tracy's schedule is read aloud: Dotcom (a bodyguard) wants to show vacation photos.
jokes.punchline: Tracy cancels it; Kenneth's 'Again' reveals this is a recurring cancellation — Dotcom's Greece photos have been perpetually postponed.
jokes.explanation: The word 'Again' at the end of Kenneth's line is doing all the work — it implies a whole history of Dotcom's perpetually-unshown Greece photos. Economy is high; the joke requires only one word to establish the running gag.

jokes.text: but she never takes off her shoes, which i kind of like. even though the reason is she's never let a man see her feet.
jokes.setup: Danny describes a romantic encounter escalating normally — then reveals his partner keeps her shoes on.
jokes.punchline: He likes the shoes-on detail; then the reason is revealed — she's never let a man see her feet, a specific and alarming neurosis that he finds sexy rather than concerning.
jokes.explanation: A two-step joke with a good structure: 'I kind of like it' is the first beat, and 'the reason is she's never let a man see her feet' recontextualizes the shoes-on detail as a quirk. The specificity of the foot issue is funny and slightly unsettling, which is the right register.

jokes.text: 'cause you know what i always say, black light attack!
jokes.setup: Jack asks Liz about her personal life. She says 'same old nothing.' He then reveals the truth with a UV light.
jokes.punchline: 'Black light attack!' — Jack produces a black light and illuminates Liz, revealing Danny's body paint glowing on her, exposing the relationship.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's title joke and it earns it. The callback to the black light party and Danny's robot body paint is elegant — all the setup was done naturally, the payoff is visually comic (Liz glowing), and 'black light attack!' as a catchphrase is absurdly quotable. The structure is excellent: Jack feigning casual interest before the reveal, the theatrical announcement, the visual gag. Episode title jokes rarely land this well.

jokes.text: yes, i've had office relationships in the past, but always with people that i could transfer to another city or introduce to nicolas sarkozy.
jokes.setup: Jack defends his past office relationships to Liz.
jokes.punchline: His criterion for appropriate office hookups: people who could be introduced to Nicolas Sarkozy — implying a level of social mobility as a qualifying factor.
jokes.explanation: The Nicolas Sarkozy criterion is exceptional Jack Donaghy character comedy — his eligibility test for romantic partners involves being presentable to a sitting French president. The specificity (Sarkozy, not just 'a European leader') makes it perfect. Only Jack would have this as a genuine romantic filter. Justifies 8+ — comparable to the best Jack lines on the show.

jokes.text: first, i don't want to go to strip clubs, and then i get angry at the hilarious dude that says something awesome.
jokes.setup: Tracy reflects on his behavior change since adding Sue to the entourage.
jokes.punchline: He describes his decent behavior as alarming dysfunction — not wanting strip clubs and defending a woman are framed as personality disorders.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's internalization of misogyny as his baseline identity — such that decency reads as malfunction — is insightful character comedy. 'Hilarious dude that says something awesome' as his description of the Italian ice comment is great ironic framing.

jokes.text: would a mother be planning a sex tour of vietnam this spring?
jokes.setup: Jenna insists she can't be a mother (the role).
jokes.punchline: Her proof of non-motherliness: a planned sex tour of Vietnam.
jokes.explanation: Only Jenna would use a sex tour as evidence of youth. The phrasing 'this spring' makes it sound like an ordinary vacation, which is the perfect deadpan touch. Very character-specific: Jenna's argument inadvertently reveals more about her than she intends.

jokes.text: you can be like Madonna and cling to youth with your gollum arms.
jokes.setup: Pete offers Jenna a choice between aging gracefully (Meryl Streep) or clinging to youth (Madonna).
jokes.punchline: 'Gollum arms' — a specific physical descriptor for Madonna's overly-muscular arms, compared to the CGI creature from Lord of the Rings.
jokes.explanation: 'Gollum arms' is a wonderfully specific and mean celebrity-roast image. The Gollum comparison works visually (long, sinewy limbs) and characterologically (desperate clinging). It's the kind of phrase that sticks.

jokes.text: look, i know we're supposed to pretape that robot v.Wade cold open tonight.
jokes.setup: Danny mentions a sketch they need to tape.
jokes.punchline: 'Robot v. Wade' — a mash-up of Roe v. Wade (the Supreme Court case) and the robot theme of the episode — is a joke sketch title that implies the robots are debating reproductive rights.
jokes.explanation: 'Robot v. Wade' is a brilliant three-word piece of wordplay — it takes a deeply serious legal/cultural touchstone and robots it. The premise of a sketch where robots debate abortion is inherently funny. Economy is near-perfect. The kind of throwaway 30 Rock joke that rewards listeners.

jokes.text: richard, would you excuse us please? / what's up? / meet me in my office in five minutes. / well, just let me change. / Mmm, no. That won't be necessary... officer.
jokes.setup: Liz pulls Danny aside to break things off, but ends up flirting instead — Danny is in his cop costume and Liz reverts to the seduction despite planning to end it.
jokes.punchline: 'That won't be necessary... officer' — Liz completely abandons her resolution and plays along with the cop costume fantasy, revealing her weakness.
jokes.explanation: The beat of Liz losing her resolve to a cop costume is very character-specific — her willpower evaporating at the sight of Danny in uniform. The elongated pause before 'officer' is the comedy, combined with the utter betrayal of her stated intentions.

jokes.text: what are you happy about? / did we get canceled?
jokes.setup: A female coworker (presumably Liz) appears uncharacteristically happy.
jokes.punchline: Pete's first instinct when someone is happy at TGS is that the show got canceled — implying the show's cancellation would be greeted as good news.
jokes.explanation: A very dark and sharp workplace commentary — the first explanation for happiness is cancellation. This is the 'maybe we'll be dead by then' energy applied to the workplace. Brief and bleak. Good economy.

jokes.text: hang on. i'm just tweeting that i ran into you. this is so tandem. / 'random,' jenna. Those kids are saying the word 'random.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is using youth slang while tweeting to perform youthfulness.
jokes.punchline: She uses 'tandem' instead of 'random' — getting the millennial slang completely wrong, which Liz has to correct.
jokes.explanation: 'Tandem' as a failed attempt at 'random' is specifically funny because it's adjacent (both multi-syllable, both end in 'om' sound) but entirely wrong. Jenna's confident delivery of incorrect slang is very character-specific — she knows she should say the young thing but doesn't know what it is.

jokes.text: um, i already turned it off.
jokes.setup: Jenna is still screaming and performing pain from the high-pitched tone.
jokes.punchline: Frank has already turned it off — meaning Jenna is performing a reaction to a stimulus that no longer exists, which implies she was performing all along.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. Five words ('um, I already turned it off') reveal Jenna was faking or that she's so committed to performance she's still reacting to nothing. The 'um' prefix adds casualness that makes the deflation perfect. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: this is from danny's chips costume. what is it doing here? / officer, what's going on up there? / it's an accident. a really bad one.
jokes.setup: Jack finds part of Danny's costume in the office. The scene cuts to Danny in a cop costume blocking Jack's access.
jokes.punchline: Danny is literally playing cop to block Jack from Liz's office — the costume becomes functional metaphor. 'A really bad one' over-sells the performance.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Danny fully committed to his cop role to block Jack is a good physical comedy moment. The stakes and commitment of 'a really bad one' as if there's a real accident is a fun extension of the bit.

jokes.text: for four years i've had to make do with what passes for men in this place. with their untucked shirts, boneless faces, their stars, both wars and trek.
jokes.setup: Liz defends her right to have Danny as a romantic interest, describing the alternative men at TGS.
jokes.punchline: 'Boneless faces, their stars, both wars and trek' — the men at TGS are characterized by nerd signifiers (Star Wars, Star Trek) and the phrase 'boneless faces' is a wonderfully specific insult.
jokes.explanation: 'Boneless faces' is an extraordinary insult — specific, visual, and almost biological in its dismissiveness. 'Their stars, both wars and trek' is a beautifully economical way to cover both sci-fi fandoms in four words, with the word 'both' doing enormous work. This line encapsulates the writers' room environment perfectly. Among the episode's best lines — the originality and economy are exceptional. Justifies 8+ easily.

jokes.text: and now i'm at the point where i love just kissing. we kiss for an hour, and it's totally enough for me.
jokes.setup: Jack and Danny are supposed to be having 'guy talk' about Danny's romantic life.
jokes.punchline: Jack has devolved into describing his own romantic preferences — kissing for an hour being 'totally enough' — in the context of a bros-talking-about-girls conversation. This is Jack's competitive, needy side.
jokes.explanation: Jack inserting his own romantic preferences into what was meant to be Danny's story is a good character reveal — he can't help making himself the subject. The specific detail ('an hour') and 'totally enough for me' as a statement of contentment is slightly sad and very funny.

jokes.text: you know, my little cuddlebaby loves to watch figure skating, and i'm really starting to get into that.
jokes.setup: Danny suggests they forget about girls and just watch the game. Jack responds about his new romantic interest.
jokes.punchline: 'Little cuddlebaby' — Jack's term of endearment in the context of guy talk is unexpected and sweet, but the figure skating detail is funnier: Jack Donaghy, titan of industry, getting into figure skating for a woman.
jokes.explanation: Jack calling someone 'little cuddlebaby' in a bros-bonding context reveals his softer side in a funny way. 'I'm really starting to get into that' (figure skating) as Jack's concession to romance is character-specific and gently absurd.

jokes.text: that was a low blow last night, lemon. / what can i say, jack? i guess i'm getting a second wind here at the tail end of my dirty 30s.
jokes.setup: Jack complains about last night's events.
jokes.punchline: Liz uses the 'dirty 30s' phrase from the TV segment (which Jack presumably also watched), smugly reframing her sexual vitality as a medical phenomenon.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Liz co-opting the 'dirty 30s' framing to justify her situation is funny and character-specific. The phrase 'second wind at the tail end' adds a sense of urgency/desperation that is very Liz.

tmdb_overview: Jack tries to squash the burgeoning relationship between Liz and Danny. Tracy asks Sue to be in his entourage. Jenna tries out for Gossip Girl.
insight: Season 4's densest episode: 63 jokes in 22 minutes, led by character escalation.
